items.concept: past ages with a fixed gap
items.micro_skill: relate a past age ratio to ages today
items.stem: A mother is 21 years older than her son. Five years ago, the mother was four times as old as her son. How old is the son today?

reveal.terms: An age difference stays the same as both people grow older.
reveal.shortcut: Five years ago the mother was 4 times the son's age, so the 21-year gap is 3 of the son's ages then: 21 ÷ 3 = 7. Add the 5 years back: 7 + 5 = 12.
reveal.why_correct: 12 years is right. Today the son is 12 and the mother 33. Five years ago they were 7 and 28, and 28 = 4 × 7.

why_wrong.o2: 33 years is the mother's age today, not the son's.
why_wrong.o3: 16 years is 21 − 5: it subtracts the five years from the age gap instead of using the 'four times' relation.
why_wrong.o4: 7 years is the son's age five years ago; add the 5 years back to get his age today.

method_steps.2_givens: gap 21 years; five years ago, mother = 4 × son
method_steps.3_method: Use the fixed gap. When one age is 4 times the other, the gap is 3 times the smaller age.
method_steps.4_why: The gap never changes, so it is the same 21 years five years ago.
method_steps.5_solve_by_hand: Five years ago: 4s − s = 3s = 21, so s = 7. Today: 7 + 5 = 12 years.
method_steps.6_check: Today 12 and 33 (gap 21). Five years ago 7 and 28; 4 × 7 = 28.
method_steps.7_distractors: 33 years: 33 years is the mother's age today, not the son's. 16 years: 16 years is 21 − 5: it subtracts the five years from the age gap instead of using the 'four times' relation. 7 years: 7 years is the son's age five years ago; add the 5 years back to get his age today.

items.notes: Draft revision of CIVIO-NUM-WP-ALGEBRA-926041 (reviewed). Scenario made realistic: a 12-year-old 'trainee' (7 years old five years ago) is implausible; now a mother and son. Numbers, key and distractors unchanged. Pending independent review; not approved.

revision_history.change: Scenario made realistic: a 12-year-old 'trainee' (7 years old five years ago) is implausible; now a mother and son. Numbers, key and distractors unchanged.

items.micro_skill: solve for an original amount from a fractional remainder
items.stem: A recycling shop sold 12 kilograms of plastic bottles. After the sale, the remaining stock was 3 kilograms more than half the starting stock. How many kilograms did it have at the start?

reveal.terms: Let x be the starting stock. After selling 12 kilograms, x − 12 remains.
reveal.shortcut: Set x − 12 = x/2 + 3. Move half of x to the left: x/2 = 15. Double to get x = 30.
reveal.why_correct: Starting with 30 kilograms and selling 12 leaves 18; half of 30 plus 3 is also 18.

why_wrong.o1: 24 kilograms assumes the 12 kilograms sold was exactly half the stock (12 × 2) and ignores the extra 3 kilograms in the remainder.
why_wrong.o2: 15 kilograms is half the starting stock (x/2 = 15), the middle step, not the full starting amount.
why_wrong.o4: 18 kilograms is the stock left after the sale (30 − 12 = 18), not the stock at the start.

method_steps.2_givens: sold 12 kg; left = half the start + 3 kg
method_steps.3_method: Set the two expressions for the remaining stock equal.
method_steps.4_why: The remaining stock can be written two ways: start − 12 and half the start + 3.
method_steps.7_distractors: 24 kilograms: 24 kilograms assumes the 12 kilograms sold was exactly half the stock (12 × 2) and ignores the extra 3 kilograms in the remainder. 15 kilograms: 15 kilograms is half the starting stock (x/2 = 15), the middle step, not the full starting amount. 18 kilograms: 18 kilograms is the stock left after the sale (30 − 12 = 18), not the stock at the start.
method_steps.8_shortcut: The half that was not counted equals 12 + 3 = 15, so the start is 30.

items.notes: Draft revision of CIVIO-NUM-WP-ALGEBRA-926039 (reviewed). Explanation fix: the 18-kg distractor is the stock left after the sale (30 − 12), not a sign error; 24-kg explanation made exact. Pending independent review; not approved.

revision_history.change: Explanation fix: the 18-kg distractor is the stock left after the sale (30 − 12), not a sign error; 24-kg explanation made exact.

items.concept: ages from future sum and gap
items.micro_skill: undo a future total before splitting ages
items.stem: Two cousins are 6 years apart. Four years from now their ages will total 48. How old is the younger cousin today?

reveal.terms: The age gap stays the same, but their combined age grows by two years each year.
reveal.shortcut: Four years from now the total is 48. Today it is 48 − 8 = 40. The younger age is (40 − 6) ÷ 2 = 17.
reveal.why_correct: Today the cousins are 17 and 23; in four years they will be 21 and 27, totaling 48.

why_wrong.o1: 23 years is the older cousin’s present age, not the younger one.
why_wrong.o3: 20 years is their current average age; the younger cousin is three years below it.
why_wrong.o4: 21 years is the younger cousin's age four years from now (17 + 4); the question asks for the age today.

method_steps.3_method: Undo the future: each cousin loses 4 years.
method_steps.4_why: Both cousins age, so the total falls by 8.
method_steps.6_check: 17 and 23 now; 21 and 27 in four years; 21 + 27 = 48.
method_steps.7_distractors: 23 years: 23 years is the older cousin’s present age, not the younger one. 20 years: 20 years is their current average age; the younger cousin is three years below it. 21 years: 21 years is the younger cousin's age four years from now (17 + 4); the question asks for the age today.

items.notes: Draft revision of CIVIO-NUM-WP-ALGEBRA-926042 (reviewed). Explanation fix: the 21-year distractor is the younger cousin's age four years from now (17 + 4), not a missed step. Pending independent review; not approved.

revision_history.change: Explanation fix: the 21-year distractor is the younger cousin's age four years from now (17 + 4), not a missed step.

items.micro_skill: scale output using workers and hours
items.stem: Three equally fast volunteers pack 360 relief kits in 6 hours. At the same pace, how many kits can 5 volunteers pack in 4 hours?

reveal.terms: A "volunteer-hour" is one volunteer working for one hour. At a steady pace, every volunteer-hour packs the same number of kits.
reveal.shortcut: Step 1: first crew = 3 volunteers × 6 hours = 18 volunteer-hours. Step 2: 360 kits ÷ 18 = 20 kits per volunteer-hour. Step 3: new crew = 5 × 4 = 20 volunteer-hours. Step 4: 20 × 20 = 400 kits.
reveal.why_correct: 400 kits is right: 5 volunteers × 4 hours = 20 volunteer-hours, and each volunteer-hour packs 20 kits, so 20 × 20 = 400. Check: 400 ÷ 20 = 20 volunteer-hours = 5 × 4.

why_wrong.o1: 360 kits simply repeats the production of the first crew instead of adjusting workers and time.
why_wrong.o2: 240 kits scales down to four hours but keeps only the original three volunteers.
why_wrong.o4: 600 kits accounts for five volunteers but keeps the original six-hour shift.

method_steps.1_asked: Kits packed by 5 volunteers in 4 hours.
method_steps.3_method: Find kits per volunteer per hour, then multiply by the new volunteers and hours.
method_steps.4_why: Output grows with both people and time.
method_steps.5_solve_by_hand: 3 × 6 = 18 volunteer-hours make 360 kits, so 1 volunteer-hour makes 20. New: 5 × 4 = 20 volunteer-hours → 20 × 20 = 400 kits.
method_steps.7_distractors: 360 kits: 360 kits simply repeats the production of the first crew instead of adjusting workers and time. 240 kits: 240 kits scales down to four hours but keeps only the original three volunteers. 600 kits: 600 kits accounts for five volunteers but keeps the original six-hour shift.

items.notes: Draft revision of CIVIO-NUM-WP-RATE-926043 (reviewed). Explanation fix: teach the work-rate calculation for 400 kits step by step (kits per volunteer-hour, then new volunteer-hours). Pending independent review; not approved.
